generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, presenting with authority means more than reporting a study. You are expected to take a position on what the evidence shows and to defend it, because the discipline advances by argument. A psychology audience will probe your method and your interpretation, so authority comes from knowing your evidence well enough to say what it does and does not support, and to concede the limits of a finding without abandoning your case.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology finalists present the same findings from a memory study, then take questions.

Tom has memorised his slides and delivers them fluently. When a tutor asks why he trusts an effect drawn from a single small sample, Tom repeats the result from an earlier slide and moves on. His talk was smooth, but the argument lived only on the slides. Faced with a fair question about his evidence, he had nothing to add. This is delivery without authority.

Amara presents the same findings and meets the same question directly. She acknowledges the small sample, explains why she still finds the effect plausible given a converging second study, and concedes that replication is needed before the claim is secure. The room can see she understands her evidence, not just her slides. This is authority: the case is owned, and it holds up when pushed.

Both presented the same findings. Only Amara could defend them, and that is what a psychology audience reads as authority.
generatedProse.summary: Presenting with authority in psychology means owning your evidence and defending your interpretation, not reciting a study. You can now explain what authority looks like, recognise it in how a presenter handles a probing question, and choose an authoritative response yourself. The next lesson turns from the individual to the team, and the skills collaboration asks of you.

check.body: In the worked example, what gave Amara authority that Tom lacked?

items.text: She answered the challenge directly, conceded the sample limit, and defended the effect with reasons.
She delivered the slides more smoothly than Tom did.
She spoke for longer and included more detail.
She avoided the difficult question to stay on script.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara owned her evidence and defended her interpretation when it was challenged.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the hard question, not how she delivered the slides.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara had authority because she met the challenge, conceded the sample limit, and defended the effect with reasons. Delivery and length were not the difference.
